description: “We used to look up at the sky and wonder at our place in the stars. Now we just look down, and worry about our place in the dirt.” — Cooper
summary:
**SPHEREx Explorer** is an interactive web-based platform designed to explore and analyse NASA's SPHEREx infrared observations. Users can search celestial objects using Right Ascension and Declination, retrieve available observations, and examine infrared images through an interactive viewer.

Our key features include 102-channel spectral analysis with individual spectra, multi-epoch comparison and difference spectrum graphs, along with WCS-based image differencing and variance-weighted image stacking.

A special capability of our platform is **moving-object isolation and tracking**. When a potential moving object is identified, the platform compares observations from different epochs, performs image alignment and differencing, subtracts the background and isolates the object's signal from the surrounding sky. It then displays the isolated object across observations and calculates its angular displacement and apparent motion.

The platform also integrates Gaia DR3, AllWISE and CSA NEOSSat catalogue information where available, and provides time-lapse animations of the same sky region across different observation periods.

By combining these capabilities, SPHEREx Explorer turns complex infrared observations into an interactive tool for discovering and studying changes in the universe.
details:
What It Does and How It Works

SPHEREx Explorer is a full-stack, browser-based astronomical exploration and analysis platform designed to process, analyse and visualize NASA's available SPHEREx Level-2 Multi-Extension FITS (MEF) observations. It connects to the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) to retrieve observations based on celestial coordinates. Users can enter Right Ascension and Declination or select from five predefined targets: WISE 0855-0714, Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi Ba/Bb, RW Aurigae and R Draconis.

The backend processes the FITS data using zodiacal-light subtraction when the relevant extension is available, quality-bitmask filtering, background estimation, source centroiding and World Coordinate System (WCS) reprojection. The platform provides the following capabilities:

  • 102-Channel Spectral Analysis: Provides a 102-channel infrared spectral representation across the nominal 0.75 to 5.00 micrometre wavelength range, covering detectors D1 to D6. The current prototype combines available FITS-derived measurements with model-assisted spectral interpolation. Its graph interface supports individual spectra, multi-epoch spectral comparisons and difference spectra, where later flux is compared with earlier flux.
  • Multi-Epoch Time-Lapse: Generates animated GIFs from available observations of the same sky region. It supports Fixed Sky mode, which aligns observations to fixed celestial coordinates, and Follow Object mode, which centres observations on the object's measured position. It selects observations from a common detector and attempts to maintain similar wavelengths, while reporting compatibility warnings when needed.
  • Difference Imaging: Aligns observations using WCS, estimates and matches image resolution, corrects background levels and calculates the later-minus-earlier difference image. It also produces significance maps and identifies potential residual candidates, including brightening sources, fading sources and positive-negative moving-object dipoles.
  • Variance-Weighted Image Stacking: Combines compatible observations from the same detector using inverse-variance weighting. It also measures background noise and estimates the improvement in signal-to-noise ratio.
  • Moving-Object Isolation and Tracking: Allows a potential moving object to be investigated across two observation epochs. The system subtracts the estimated background, aligns the images and applies a spatial isolation mask to emphasize the object's signal while suppressing the surrounding sky. It generates isolated images for both epochs and calculates angular displacement, time baseline and apparent motion in arcseconds per year.
  • Photometry and Catalogue Cross-Matching: Allows users to select an image position and retrieve celestial coordinates, centroid measurements, surface brightness in MJy/sr, derived point-source flux in microjanskys, signal-to-noise ratio and quality information. It decodes the 14 defined quality-bitmask categories. Catalogue integration includes proper-motion-adjusted Gaia DR3 positions, AllWISE sources and CSA NEOSSat observation information where available.
Tools, Coding Languages and Software

Backend

  • Python 3.12
  • FastAPI and Uvicorn

Scientific and Image Processing Libraries

  • Astropy for FITS handling, celestial coordinates, time calculations and WCS operations.
  • Photutils for source detection and centroiding.
  • NumPy and SciPy for numerical processing.
  • Reproject for image alignment.
  • Matplotlib and Pillow for image and animation generation.

Frontend

  • React and TypeScript for the web application and interactive interface.
  • Plotly.js for spectral graph visualization.
  • Tailwind CSS, if used in the final frontend implementation.

Astronomical Data Sources

  • NASA/IPAC IRSA for SPHEREx observations and AllWISE data.
  • Gaia DR3 for stellar astrometry and catalogue cross-matching.
  • Canadian Astronomy Data Centre (CADC) for CSA NEOSSat observation information.

The application does not require custom spacecraft hardware. It is designed to run as a software platform through a web browser.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Astronomical observation data is often stored in specialized FITS formats that require scientific programming knowledge and dedicated software to process and interpret. SPHEREx Explorer aims to simplify this process by bringing observation retrieval, image visualization, spectral analysis and multi-epoch comparison into one accessible platform.

It can support students, astronomy enthusiasts and researchers in exploring infrared observations, studying brown dwarfs, investigating variable sources and examining high-proper-motion objects. Its combination of image differencing, moving-object isolation, spectral comparisons and time-lapse visualization provides multiple ways to investigate changes in the observed sky.

The intended impact is to make complex infrared astronomical data easier to explore and encourage wider engagement with publicly available space science observations.

How the Project Is Creative

The creative aspect of SPHEREx Explorer is its combination of several scientific analysis methods in one interactive platform.

SPHEREx uses a Linear Variable Filter (LVF), which maps wavelength to position across its detector images. Full spectral coverage at a particular sky position is assembled from observations taken at different pointings over time. Our project explores how these observations can be brought together for spectral visualization and comparison.

Another distinctive feature is the moving-object analysis workflow. By combining WCS-based image differencing, residual candidate identification, background subtraction and spatial isolation, the platform helps users distinguish potential moving sources from changes in the surrounding sky. The isolated source can then be examined across observation dates and its apparent angular motion calculated.

The six-month time-lapse concept adds another dimension by turning separate astronomical observations into an animation, allowing users to visually investigate how the same region changes over time.

Factors Our Team Considered
  • Survey Cadence and Observation Availability: SPHEREx observations are not necessarily available at uniform intervals for every sky location. We considered variations in observation dates, detector coverage and wavelength sampling when grouping observations into epochs and generating comparisons. The application reports when adequate multi-epoch or compatible observation coverage is unavailable.
  • Data Quality and Edge Cases: FITS data may contain missing pixels, flagged detector regions, non-finite values and unusually high pixel readings. We incorporated quality-bitmask filtering, background statistics, isolated-spike rejection and handling of invalid pixels to make image processing more robust.
  • Wavelength and Detector Compatibility: Different detectors cover different wavelength ranges. We considered detector identity and wavelength compatibility when selecting observations for image stacking, difference imaging and time-lapse generation. Compatibility warnings help avoid misleading comparisons.
  • Image Alignment and Scientific Consistency: Observations taken at different pointings may have different image orientations and pixel coordinates. WCS reprojection, background correction and image-resolution matching are used to bring compatible images onto a common reference grid.
  • Network Requests and Performance: Retrieving large FITS observations can take time and create repeated network requests. We incorporated local caching, selective exposure sampling and retry logic to reduce redundant downloads and improve processing efficiency.

Our overall approach is to make the platform scientifically informative while keeping the user experience simple and accessible.
